paras: The reported slave sale at Fairview, West Virginia, was an auction of Black men and women described as "the regular annual sale of slaves," said to have been held in front of the Fairview court house on a Saturday in late March 1881. The claim rested on a single special telegram relayed through Pittsburgh and reprinted in a few Northern papers. The first paper to print it suggested the correspondent had mistaken the contracting of convict labor for a slave sale.

According to the telegram, as carried in a Pittsburg dispatch of March 29, slavery still existed in that part of the state and "regular sales of negroes" took place, "the blacks not seeming to know their rights." The correspondent cited a sale held "last Saturday" before the court house, which had been "extensively advertised" as the annual sale of slaves. It reportedly drew no unusual notice, and few attended except people who wished to buy or sell.

A number of Black men and women were put up and auctioned, bringing between $80 and $160, the highest prices paid for the "young and strong." The correspondent said some of those sold complained not of the sale but of "inhuman treatment," and some hoped new masters would treat them better.
No local West Virginia report, official statement, denial or follow-up appears in the coverage found.

The daily gazette printed the dispatch on March 31 under the headline "Strange Statements" and added a bracketed editor's note. That note said the correspondent had probably mistaken "the public contracting to the highest bidder for the labor of convicts," a practice the editor believed prevailed in West Virginia.

On April 6 the Vermont Watchman and State Journal repeated it in its weekly news summary as a "remarkable statement," without prices or comment. The next day the Princeton Union of Minnesota ran it under "Slave Sale in Virginia," calling it "among the sensations from West Virginia" and crediting a Pittsburgh paper.
Only the condensed Princeton Union version said the sale was conducted "by the local authorities"; the fuller Gazette text named no one in charge.

reader.title: Reported slave sale at Fairview, West Virginia
bases: The telegram described Black men and women auctioned as 'slaves' for a price and complaining of 'inhuman treatment' by masters (A1, A2, A3), a claim of coerced labor; A1's editor thought it was more likely the contracting of convict labor.

All three items trace to one special telegram from Fairview relayed through Pittsburgh (A1, A2, A3); no local report, denial, or follow-up was found, and A1's editor doubted the telegram's reading of what took place.
